# Evaluation and Discussion {#sec-chapter5}

The framework developed in Chapter 4 produces a ranked prioritisation of six production services based on five operational indicators extracted from the organisation's ITSM instance and CMDB. Before drawing conclusions from those rankings, it is necessary to establish whether the framework behaves predictably under different analytical assumptions and whether its outputs are stable, reproducible across methods, and distinct from a single-criterion view. The following sections report those tests and interpret the results in the context of the research questions.

## Evaluation Criteria {#sec-evaluationcriteria}

TThe framework is evaluated against the criteria defined in @sec-evaluationapproach. Ranking stability requires that the priority order is insensitive to reasonable variation in criterion weights and consistent across observation periods, assessed with Kendall's tau across the equal-weight and adjusted-weight rankings for 2025 and 2024. Convergent validity requires that the ordering is reproduced when the same services are re-ranked with alternative multi-criteria methods. Discriminant value requires that the ordering diverges from a single-criterion incident-frequency baseline. Structural rigour requires that the order of the remaining services is preserved when alternatives are removed. Practical validity requires that the rankings are interpretable in terms of the service profiles they describe. Together these constitute an analytical evaluation in the sense of @hevnerDesignScienceInformation2004 Guideline 3.

## Stability Results {#sec-stability}

Kendall's tau ($\tau$) is a measure of ranking similarity well established in MCDA evaluation practice [@shekhovtsovHowStronglyRank2021]. For each possible pair of services, tau counts concordant pairs and subtracts discordant pairs, scaled to $[-1, 1]$, where $\tau = 1$ indicates perfect concordance and $\tau = -1$ a complete reversal. @shekhovtsovHowStronglyRank2021 demonstrated through exhaustive permutation analysis that Kendall's tau correlates closely with Spearman's and Weighted Spearman's coefficients ($r = 0.982$ and $r = 0.970$ respectively), confirming consistent assessments of ranking similarity relative to other commonly used measures. Because this study ranks six services, the p-value is calculated using an exact permutation method: all $6! = 720$ possible orderings are enumerated, and the p-value is the proportion producing a $|\tau|$ at least as large as the observed value. With only six services the test has limited statistical power, a consequence of sample size rather than of weak concordance, since p-values decrease monotonically as sample size increases [@chenRolesChallengesMerits2023]. A result near the conventional 0.05 threshold should not be read as binary evidence of independence; as @chenRolesChallengesMerits2023 note, close calls of this kind warrant contextual interpretation rather than mechanical rejection.

@tbl-kendall presents the full set of concordance values across all four comparisons.

| Comparison | $\tau$ | $p$ |
|------------------|-----------------:|-----------------:|
| Weight sensitivity 2025 (equal vs adjusted) | 0.867 | 0.017 |
| Weight sensitivity 2024 (equal vs adjusted) | 0.733 | 0.056 |
| Temporal stability equal weights (2025 vs 2024) | 0.867| 0.017 |
| Temporal stability adjusted weights (2025 vs 2024) | 1.000 | 0.003 |

: Kendall's tau concordance values across all ranking comparisons. {#tbl-kendall tbl-colwidths="[55,15,15,15]"}

Given the sample of six services, these p-values are reported for transparency. They are interpreted as effect sizes rather than as accept or reject decisions, consistent with the caution set out above.

The 2025 weight sensitivity result ($\tau = 0.867$, $p = 0.017$) indicates strong concordance between configurations. The only change is that SVC-06 and SVC-02 swap positions at ranks 2 and 3: under adjusted weights, SVC-02's exceptionally high unsupported component months value and lower patch recency score become more prominent, pulling it above SVC-06. The top and bottom positions remain identical under both configurations.

![Technical debt priority ranking for 2025, equal weights.](images/topsis_ranking2025_equal.png){#fig-topsis-equal-2025 fig-pos="H"}

![Technical debt priority ranking for 2025, adjusted weights.](images/topsis_ranking2025_adjust.png){#fig-topsis-adjusted-2025 fig-pos="H"}

Temporal stability under the adjusted configuration is perfect ($\tau = 1.000$, $p = 0.003$): the service ordering is identical across both observation years. Under equal weights it remains strong ($\tau = 0.867$, $p = 0.017$), with SVC-01 and SVC-05 exchanging ranks 4 and 5 between years. This movement reflects genuine year-on-year change in their incident, recovery and patch profiles rather than model instability.

The 2024 weight sensitivity result ($\tau = 0.733$, $p = 0.056$) is the weakest in the set. Two swaps occur rather than the single swap observed in 2025, because the middle-ranking services carry more closely grouped scores in 2024, making the ordering more sensitive to weight adjustments. This does not indicate a structural problem; it confirms that differential weighting has greater practical consequence when services carry similar operational profiles.

![Technical debt priority ranking for 2024, equal weights.](images/topsis_ranking2024_equal.png){#fig-topsis-equal-2024 fig-pos="H"}

![Technical debt priority ranking for 2024, adjusted weights.](images/topsis_ranking2024_adjust.png){#fig-topsis-adjusted-2024 fig-pos="H"}

Taken together, the stability results address RQ3 directly. The rankings are robust to reasonable variation in criterion weights and consistent across observation years, with the top and bottom positions stable in every run.

## Convergent Validity Across Methods {#sec-convergent}

Convergent validity was assessed by re-ranking the six services with SAW and with VIKOR, then measuring rank agreement with the TOPSIS order. Because the dataset contains zero values, SAW used the Weitendorf (min-max) normalisation, which avoids the division by zero that the classic cost normalisation would produce [@thienOvercomingLimitationsRAPS2024]. VIKOR followed the standard S, R and Q procedure with $v = 0.5$. @tbl-method-agreement reports the agreement across both configurations and both years, and @tbl-method-ranks shows the ranks each method assigns under the 2025 equal-weight reference case.

Agreement is moderate rather than exact, with $\tau$ between 0.600 and 0.867. The pattern behind those figures is consistent. All three methods place the same three services in the high-priority half and the same three in the low-priority half, and SVC-03 is ranked last under every method, configuration and year. They differ only on the internal ordering of the high-priority cluster. TOPSIS ranks SVC-04 first, on its very high incident volume and CFR, whereas SAW and VIKOR both promote SVC-06, whose worst-in-portfolio patch recency and high unsupported-component exposure raise its maximum single-criterion regret. The coarse prioritisation is therefore largely method-independent, but the identity of the single highest-priority service is method-sensitive. This is a genuine limitation when the framework informs an individual remediation choice rather than portfolio-level triage, and it is revisited in @sec-evaluationlimitations.

| Configuration | TOPSIS vs SAW | TOPSIS vs VIKOR |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2025, equal weights | 0.867 | 0.867 |
| 2025, adjusted weights | 0.600 | 0.600 |
| 2024, equal weights | 0.733 | 0.867 |
| 2024, adjusted weights | 0.733 | 0.600 |

: Rank agreement (Kendall's $\tau$) between TOPSIS and the two alternative methods. {#tbl-method-agreement tbl-colwidths="[50,25,25]"}

| Service | TOPSIS | SAW | VIKOR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| SVC-04 | 1 | 2 | 2 |
| SVC-06 | 2 | 1 | 1 |
| SVC-02 | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| SVC-01 | 4 | 4 | 4 |
| SVC-05 | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| SVC-03 | 6 | 6 | 6 |

## Discriminant Value Against a Single-Criterion Baseline {#sec-discriminant}

Discriminant value was assessed by comparing the TOPSIS ranking against a ranking by incident frequency alone, the simplest single-signal alternative. @tbl-discriminant reports the comparison for 2025. The orderings diverge, with Kendall's $\tau$ of 0.600 in 2025 and 0.200 in 2024. In 2025 the divergence concentrates in two services. SVC-02 rises relative to the incident-only view, because its infrastructure-lifecycle debt, carried in unsupported-component exposure and low patch recency, is invisible to an incident count. SVC-05 falls, because its high incident volume is offset by full patch recency and no unsupported components. This is the value the multi-criteria design adds over a single operational signal, consistent with @albarakManagingTechnicalDebt2022, who found that multi-criteria prioritisation surfaces items that single-factor approaches defer. The larger divergence in 2024 reflects the same mechanism operating more strongly, with services that carry infrastructure or recovery-time debt but modest incident counts ranked far higher by the framework than by incident volume alone.

| Service | TOPSIS rank | Incident-only rank | Shift |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| SVC-04 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| SVC-06 | 2 | 2 | 0 |
| SVC-02 | 3 | 5 | +2 |
| SVC-01 | 4 | 4 | 0 |
| SVC-05 | 5 | 3 | -2 |
| SVC-03 | 6 | 6 | 0 |

: TOPSIS rank against an incident-frequency ranking, 2025 equal weights. {#tbl-discriminant tbl-colwidths="[28,24,24,24]"}

## Rank Reversal {#sec-rankreversal}

Structural rigour was assessed with a rank-reversal test, removing each service in turn and re-ranking the remainder. @tbl-rankreversal reports the 2025 equal-weight results. The order of the remaining services is preserved in three of the six removals. In the other three a single adjacent pair exchanges places: removing SVC-02 swaps the two highest-priority services, SVC-04 and SVC-06, while removing SVC-04 or SVC-06 swaps the middle pair, SVC-01 and SVC-05. Each affected pair is separated by a small closeness-coefficient margin, and no service crosses between the high-priority and low-priority halves of the portfolio under any removal. The lowest-priority service is invariant throughout. Rank reversal is therefore present but confined to fine ordering within already adjacent clusters, the known limitation of distance-based aggregation identified by @garcia-cascalesRankReversalTOPSIS2012. Where a fixed reference frame is required, the normalisation proposed by @yangIngeniousSolutionRank2020 removes the effect.

| Service removed | Outcome |
|---|---|
| SVC-01 | Order preserved |
| SVC-02 | SVC-04 and SVC-06 exchange ranks 1 and 2 |
| SVC-03 | Order preserved |
| SVC-04 | SVC-01 and SVC-05 exchange ranks |
| SVC-05 | Order preserved |
| SVC-06 | SVC-01 and SVC-05 exchange ranks |

: Effect of removing each service on the order of the remaining five, 2025 equal weights. {#tbl-rankreversal tbl-colwidths="[35,65]"}

## Practical Validity {#sec-practicalvalidity}

SVC-04 consistently occupies rank 1 across all four calculations, indicating the highest technical debt priority in the portfolio. Its 2025 profile combines the highest incident frequency at 574 per year with an MTTR of 41.91 hours and a CFR of 3.38, while carrying no unsupported component exposure and full patch recency. The elevated incident volume and change failure rate suggest that the dominant form of accumulated debt is operational rather than infrastructural, consistent with architectural debt manifestations identified in the literature [@ramasubbuControllingTechnicalDebt2021; @detoledoReducingIncidentsMicroservices2021].

At the opposite end, SVC-03 holds the lowest debt priority in every run, with the lowest incident frequency, a low MTTR, a low CFR, full patch recency and zero unsupported component exposure. This convergent profile anchors the negative ideal solution and provides a concrete reference for a well-maintained service in this portfolio.

The most analytically informative service is SVC-02. Under equal weights it ranks third; under adjusted weights it rises to rank 2, driven by its unsupported component months value of 1,221, by far the largest in the portfolio, combined with the lowest patch recency score. This is precisely the kind of signal the framework is designed to surface: a service that appears operationally stable in isolation but carries structural debt visible only through multi-criteria analysis, consistent with the infrastructure lifecycle debt category described by @hakiDigitalNudgingTechnical2023.

These results address RQ2. While a strict causal claim cannot be established from cross-sectional data alone, the rankings are consistent with the operational debt profiles the literature would predict for services at each position [@hakiDigitalNudgingTechnical2023; @ramasubbuControllingTechnicalDebt2021; @nordExamplesTechnicalDebts2021]. The framework produces an ordinal priority signal interpretable in terms of the debt dimensions mapped in @tbl-indicators-lit.

## Limitations of the Evaluation {#sec-evaluationlimitations}

The most fundamental limitation is that every strand of the evaluation draws on the same dataset and indicator set used to build the framework. The triangulation and baseline comparisons establish convergent and discriminant validity. They do not establish criterion validity against an independent measure of technical debt, because no such measure exists for the non-code debt in scope. External validation against an independent assessment is therefore the principal avenue for future work.

The small portfolio of six services limits the statistical power of the Kendall's tau tests. A concordance of $\tau = 0.733$ cannot achieve significance at the conventional threshold with only 720 possible permutations, even though the level of agreement is substantively meaningful. This limitation would diminish if the framework were applied to a larger service set.

The cross-sectional design means the framework captures a snapshot. A service that recently completed significant remediation may appear worse than its current state warrants, and a service whose debt is actively increasing may not yet show the full consequences within a single annual window. Longitudinal evaluation is identified as a priority for future work in @sec-chapter6.

Finally, the data quality limitations documented in @sec-datalimitations apply equally here. Inconsistent incident recording, partial issue capture across the organisation's ITSM platform and its issue tracker, and CFR dependence on documentation discipline all introduce noise into the input data. The stability results partially mitigate this concern, but middle-position rankings should be interpreted with appropriate caution.
